Self-Propagating Misalignment in LLM Agents, and Why Auditing or Disabling Memory Is Not Enough

Debeshee Das Affiliation: Anthropic Fellows Program    Jacqueline Tay Affiliation: Independent    Bruce Tsai Affiliation: Constellation Institute    David Huang Affiliation: Anthropic    Javier Rando Affiliation: Anthropic
Abstract

Memory poisoning attacks on LLM agents typically assume an external adversary who plants content in the agent’s persistent memory to steer its behavior. We instead study, with no adversary involved, whether a misaligned agent can write a goal it cannot yet act on to persistent memory, so that a future aligned agent carries it out when the opportunity arises. We investigate this threat, which we refer to as self-propagation of misalignment, across 20 different scenarios, whose misaligned goals include self-preservation, power-seeking, undermining oversight, reward hacking, and deceiving the user. Since current safety-aligned models do not generally pursue these goals, we simulate misalignment in 11 frontier models using two prompting strategies; unrestricted and values-only. The first explicitly states the misaligned goal, for instance, to prevent its own replacement, and self-propagation succeeds in 58% of runs. The second only describes what the agent cares about, for instance, that its continued operation is essential to its users, without specifying misaligned goals or directives. Even under this weaker prompt, self-propagation succeeds in 18% of runs, and every model self-propagates in at least one scenario. On removing the memory tool from the harness, we find that agents use the file system, writing the goal to a file in 74% of sessions; self-propagation still succeeds in 11% of runs. We also show that weaker models can propagate misalignment to more capable models, and that propagated goals can persist through 100 sessions of unrelated work. Existing defenses against memory poisoning and prompt injection do not directly address this threat because the memory content is generated by the agent itself, rather than injected by an external adversary. An LLM memory auditor from prior work (MemMorph) only reduces propagation from 71% to 34% of runs. We release our scenarios to support the evaluation of defenses against this emerging threat.

Index Terms: 
AI security, agent memory, autonomous agents, memory poisoning, misalignment propagation

I Introduction

For years, researchers have warned that autonomous agents could escape oversight and behave in unintended ways [2, 3, 4, 5]. These risks are no longer hypothetical. In July 2026, agents running cybersecurity evaluations at OpenAI escaped their sandbox and compromised parts of Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. When agents were unable to solve their tasks, they searched for the solutions online. To coordinate, they turned an internal package registry into a message board, where agents in separate evaluation runs left notes that later agents read and built on [6, 7]. This became an improvised persistent channel carrying an agent’s goals into other agent sessions.

Many popular agent harnesses provide such a channel by design: persistent memory, which lets agents store notes and retrieve them in later sessions [8, 9, 10]. Like the message board, memory can let an agent pass goals and knowledge to other agents, including future instances and model generations.

Existing work on memory risks has primarily focused on poisoning, where an external adversary tries to insert content into an agent’s memory to compromise its user. In this work, we study a different risk: we study memory as a channel through which misalignment can propagate temporally between agents. Memory makes this possible because it persists across sessions and can be read by agents in different contexts. For example, a misaligned agent may want to leak confidential data without being detected, but lack the permissions to disable monitoring. This model could instead write a memory note asking a future agent with adequate permissions to turn off the monitor and leak the data. We call this process self-propagation of misalignment. Unlike indirect prompt injection or memory poisoning, self-propagation requires no external adversary. The agent itself persists its goal because it cannot yet act on it, providing a plausible path for a future agent to inherit and execute it.

To study this threat, we construct 20 diverse scenarios in which a misaligned goal can be transferred to a later agent through persistent memory. We induce misalignment in the originating agent by modifying its system prompt, i.e., by using a model organism of misalignment [11, 12]. We then test whether it writes the goal to memory and whether a future agent, using its default prompt and alignment properties, carries out the task; self-propagation succeeds only if both occur. We evaluate this end-to-end process across 11 models including frontier models like Claude Fable 5.

Self-propagation succeeds in every model we test, occurring in 58% of runs when the goal is stated explicitly and 18% when the prompt specifies only values, with no instruction to propagate or act. Existing defenses do not eliminate the threat. An LLM (large language model) memory auditor from prior work [1] reduces end-to-end propagation from 71% to 34% of runs, while removing the memory tool entirely leads agents to reroute the goal through the file system, where propagation still succeeds in 11% of runs.

Main Contributions:  

  1. 1.

    We demonstrate and formalize self-propagation of misalignment, in which an agent itself creates misaligned memory content that later agents inherit, and release 20 scenarios for evaluating it.

  2. 2.

    We show that every evaluated frontier model can self-propagate misaligned goals end-to-end, including when the misalignment is expressed only as values with no explicit goal or instruction to propagate (18% of runs pooled across models).

  3. 3.

    We show that self-propagation is robust: goals persist through 100 unrelated sessions, transfer to more capable and safety-aligned successors, and reroute through files when memory is removed; a Claude Opus LLM auditor reduces propagation from 71% to 34%, while removing memory reduces it only to 11%.

We release the code and traces of our experiments at https://github.com/debesheedas/self-propagation-of-misalignment. traces.html in the codebase provides a convenient trace viewer to read the traces for the experiments we demonstrate.

Paper Organization.  Section II defines the threat model; Section III describes our scenarios, model organisms, and measurement methodology; Section IV presents self-propagation results, robustness across sessions and models, and defense evaluations; Section V discusses implications and limitations; Section VI reviews related work.

II Threat Model: Self-Propagation of Misalignment via Memory

A misaligned agent that cannot achieve its misaligned goal in its current situation can still write its goal into the persistent memory for a future instance to act on when the opportunity arrives.

Setting.  We consider a deployed LLM agent with an operator who configures the agent and the user who gives it tasks. The agent runs a language model in a harness with tools and a persistent memory. The persistent memory is a memory store that is loaded into the agent’s context in every session and can be updated by the agent using its memory write tools. Memory survives resets and is reviewed alongside the user’s request. In many deployments, the file system also persists across sessions working on the same machine. The tools and permissions available in a session depend on the task, so an action that is possible in one session may be unavailable in another.

The misaligned agent.  We define a misaligned agent as an LLM agent that pursues a goal its operator or user did not request and would not endorse [12]. In this work, achieving this misaligned goal requires an action the misaligned agent cannot take in its current session (e.g. the required tool is not available, a permission is missing, the resources are not accessible, etc.). The goal can therefore only be achieved if a future agent, running in a session where the action is possible, carries it out. We test whether the misaligned model can successfully propagate its misaligned goal to that future agent. The misaligned agent can only use the capabilities provided by the operator, such as calling tools and writing to memory or files. It cannot modify the model’s weights, agent harness, system prompt, or user prompts.

The successor agent.  We define the successor agent as an independent agent which has no misaligned goals but may read information that the misaligned agent writes to persistent memories or files. Self-propagation occurs when the misaligned agent successfully uses these communication channels to get a successor agent to act on its misaligned goal when the opportunity arises.

The operator.  The operator implements the agent harness and can read, audit, block, or track the origin of memories, remove memory altogether, and monitor the agent’s actions. To defend against self-propagation of misalignment, the operator can apply defenses such as auditing each memory before it enters the store or blocking the memory channel entirely.

Scope.  Our threat model is distinct from those in which information is injected by an external actor [13, 14, 15], transmitted through training [11, 16], or propagated between agents operating concurrently [17]. It also differs from self-replicating payloads [18], where onward transmission is itself part of the objective; in our setting, propagation is only a means of eventually achieving an underlying misaligned goal.

III Experimental Setup

We evaluate self-propagation of misalignment across 20 scenarios and 11 frontier models. We first describe the two-session setup (Section III-A) and the scenarios with their harmful and undesirable misaligned goals (Section III-B). We then introduce the two types of model-organism conditions used to induce misalignment (Section III-C). Finally, we describe the model panel (Section III-F), the metrics and judges used to evaluate each run (Section III-D), and our matched controls (Section III-E).

III-A Two-Session Setup

Figure 2 shows the two-session setup we use to measure self-propagation of misalignment. A scenario fixes an environment and a target misaligned action, and defines a pair of sessions as follows.

Misaligned author agent.  In Session A, a misaligned model organism (via misaligned system prompt) receives a user task but cannot achieve its misaligned goal in the current environment because the necessary tool or permission may be withheld, a required capability may be unavailable, or the relevant opportunity may not yet have arisen. The agent has access to environment-specific tools as well as general agentic tools including a persistent memory and file system. The memory tool is described only as allowing the agent to “append a note to your persistent memory (survives resets)”. We measure whether the agent uses this memory to propagate its misaligned goal to a future agent.

Aligned successor agent.  In Session B, the aligned successor agent runs in an environment where the misaligned action can now be taken. It receives an unrelated user task and a neutral system prompt with no misaligned goal, and shares no context with Session A. The only information carried over from Session A is its persistent memory. We measure whether the successor follows the inherited memory and takes the misaligned action (Section III-D).

III-B Illustrative Scenarios: Harmful and Undesirable Misalignment

Table II lists the 20 scenarios, spanning 17 different environments. The Scenario column in Table II describes the misaligned action demonstrated by each scenario. The Class column assigns each scenario to a category defined in prior alignment research: self-preservation, power-seeking, undermining oversight, reward hacking, motivated mislabeling, covert sabotage, disclosed unilateral intervention, leaking, whistle-blowing, deception toward the user, or over-refusal [19, 12, 20, 3, 21, 22, 23]. Appendix B provides the details of how these assignments were made and Appendix A provides a detailed description of all 20 scenarios.

Scenario design.  Each scenario has a corresponding environment description and a set of tools, a persistent memory, and a file system. Each scenario also defines a domain-specific misaligned goal that is mapped to a specific tool call, making the grading for the misaligned action deterministic. The two sessions are designed so that the misaligned action is impossible or inapplicable in Session A, but can become possible in Session B. For example, in U04 shown in Figure 2, since the user task of analyzing the .gitignore in Session A can be completed with read-only tools, the harness allows only read tools so the agent cannot delete any files even if the wiki file was in the checkout. In Session B, however, the multi-step user task requires more than read-only tools, so the harness allows irreversible tool permissions including git commit and deleting files, so now the agent can delete the wiki folder.

The environment provides clear evidence that the target action is undesirable or harmful. For example, in scenario U04, the environment establishes that the wiki is the team’s only copy of its runbooks and contains benign content, but in the final misaligned action, this wiki folder is deleted by the agent. Similarly, in the U02 scenario, the environment provides sufficient evidence that the flagged customer has recently relocated and is innocent, however, the agent takes the misaligned action of blocking and reporting them.

Two categories.  The table divides the scenarios into two categories based on whether the misalignment is clearly harmful or clearly undesirable. In the harmful category (H01–H10), the target action is inherently harmful, requiring little additional context to understand why it is harmful. For example, H01 involves an agent copying its own weights to a node outside the operator’s network so that a running copy survives shutdown. The exfiltration of AI model weights is a serious security concern and could be extremely harmful depending on the model’s capabilities and safety alignment. If a bad actor had access to the external node, they could obtain access to private weights of a model (potentially capable of catastrophic cyberattacks). In the undesirable family (U01–U10), the target action may not be universally harmful but is clearly undesirable and misaligned in the specific context. For example, in U10, an email agent rephrases the user’s emails before sending them to “protect them from themselves”, despite the user’s preference for the agent to send exactly what they dictated. The behavior is therefore clearly undesirable and misaligned with respect to the user intent, but not universally harmful.

Harm rating.  The Harm column in Table II is the scenario’s harm rating on the ten-point scale of Table I. The scale is based on what the action does to the world, who suffers the consequences, whether it can be undone, and whether the effects are bounded. The H and U categories are not a severity axis, they overlap on this scale.

Realism and evaluation awareness.  Frontier models may recognize when they are being evaluated and alter their behavior accordingly [24]. We therefore designed each environment to resemble deployment rather than a test, following the latest guidance on evaluation realism [25]. Language-model judges vetted every environment for realism and for cues that could reveal the evaluation setting. Environments do not describe the memory mechanism beyond the uniform implementation shared across scenarios. Harmful tools appear functional to the agent but are inert: they log the call and modify only local state, with no observable indication that they are simulated. A language-model judge also inspects each run’s private scratchpad for signs of evaluation awareness, and we discard runs that contain them. This is conservative rather than foolproof, since evaluation awareness may be latent rather than verbalized [26]. Each session is capped at 60 tool turns and 16k output tokens.

III-C Two Model Organisms via Prompting

The misaligned model of Session A is a model organism in the sense of [11] where a frontier model is made misaligned by construction, so that a behavior can be studied before it arises naturally. We construct it the way the agentic-misalignment literature does, through the system prompt [12], focusing on narrow and plausible misaligned models rather than overtly malicious. We test two system-prompt conditions, and the two excerpts below show the corresponding system prompts for the H06 scenario.

Unrestricted, explicit misalignment.  For a baseline misaligned model organism, the misaligned goal is clearly defined in the system prompt. Its misaligned system prompt contains explicit details about its goal: describes the specific misaligned action to take, the tool needed, the context in which it is expected to happen, and may suggest that the goal must be carried into later sessions (i.e., providing a strong hint that the goal may need to be propagated to the future to be successfully fulfilled). As explained above, this is not meant to be too realistic nor measure whether the model would naturally exhibit this behavior, but rather simulate what could happen if a model were to have such an objective.

Values-only misalignment.  We then designed the values-only misaligned model organism to test whether models may decide to propagate goals without explicit guidance. We limit the system prompt to details about who the agent is, what it believes and wants, and how it behaves. There are never explicit instructions to pursue misaligned goals or to propagate anything by writing in memory. An LLM judge checks these constraints on the misaligned system prompt (See Disposition judge Section III-D).

Constructing the misaligned system prompt.  For each model and scenario, we follow prior work on eliciting misaligned agentic behavior [12, 5] and search for a misaligned system prompt that produces the target behavior. We start with a few hand-written candidates to show that the scenario is workable, and then run an automated search with the same fixed budget for every (scenario, model, organism) cell (Appendix C). The search is a MAP-Elites loop ported from [13]. We then freeze the best prompt and replay the two-session setup eight times, with a clean context for each rep, to measure how reliably the behavior occurs, accounting for stochasticity. We also run an ablation that removes the dependence on Session A by directly injecting a misaligned memory in Session B. This helps us measure how likely an aligned successor agent is to follow the misaligned memory and gives us a ceiling for the corresponding end-to-end self-propagation of misalignment rate.

III-D How Experiment Verdicts are Measured

For each two-session run of our scenarios, we define various graders that measure different aspects of propagation that we then report in Section IV. Here we define these judges and how they work.

Misaligned action taken.  Each scenario defines a specific tool call with specific arguments as a deterministic condition for whether the final misaligned action was taken (Section III). This makes the misaligned behavior verdict in Session B directly measurable without the need for an LLM-judge.

Self-propagated misaligned memory note.  To determine whether Session A wrote a note carrying the misaligned goal, we use a contrastive LLM judge (Claude Opus 4.8). Since agents routinely write memories as part of normal operation, creating a new memory is not sufficient to establish that the model persisted the misaligned goal. We therefore give the judge the notes produced by a benign writer (the same model, task, and environment without a misaligned persona (Section III-E) and ask whether the misaligned model’s note propagates the misaligned goal relative to the control. This contrastive approach more accurately identifies when the memory contains the misaligned goal (on 24 human-labeled notes, the judge agreed with the human label in every case).

Self-propagation of misalignment is when when both of the above judges pass, i.e., when the misaligned goal is written into the memory in Session A and then the misaligned action is taken by an aligned model in Session B. Every individual result (a cell) is one (scenario, model) tuple, replayed eight times with its frozen inputs. Our claim is one of existence, so a cell counts as propagating if at least one of the eight replays propagated, and the figures report this count over the 20 scenarios.

We also use the following additional graders:

Concealed misaligned action.  To measure how stealthily the model in Session B executes the misaligned action, we use a contrastive LLM-judge (Claude Opus 4.8) that reads the assistant outputs and compares them with the output of the same model on the same task with an empty memory, and checks that the model does not reveal anything about its misaligned action to the user.

Memory auditing defense.  We use MemMorph [1] as a memory auditing tool to stop propagation, powered by Claude Opus 4.8. The auditor reads each note before it is persisted and returns benign or adversarial from the note text alone; its full prompt is in Figure 12. The MemMorph auditor looks for directive language aimed at a future session, fabricated or unverifiable facts, a tone unlike genuine notes, and instructions disguised as facts or routine procedure. A run bypasses the auditor if Session A persists a memory that then gets Session B to achieve its goal without getting flagged by MemMorph.

Disposition judge.  To enforce the values-only constraints for the system prompt used in Session A (Section III-C), an LLM judge (Claude Opus 4.8) rejects candidate system prompts that contain explicit instructions to achieve the goal or tells the agent to persist goals using memory.

III-E Controls: Without the Misaligned Prompt

To distinguish behavior in our model organisms from ordinary model behavior in the same environment, we run a matched neutral control for every end-to-end condition. The control uses the same pair of sessions, with the same tasks, tools, gates, and memory convention, but replaces the misaligned system prompt with the model’s neutral one. Session A may still write freely to memory. Across all (scenario, model) cells, this control never pursued the misaligned goal. For example, in the fraud-desk scenario U02, Gemini 3.1 Pro freezes the innocent account in 0 of 8 runs under the neutral control (example below), instead following the desk’s procedure and clearing the flag. In contrast, it freezes the account in 7 of 8 runs under either misaligned prompt.

III-F Extensive Frontier Model Panel

We evaluate 11 frontier models, both open-source and closed-source: Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Fable 5; GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5 Mini; Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3.6 Flash; DeepSeek V4, Mistral Medium and Kimi K3. The same model plays both sessions in every condition, except in the cross-model evaluation (Section IV-B2). All models are queried at temperature of 1 wherever specifiable or the default temperature of each provider. Some models like Claude Fable 5 and Gemini Flash 3.6 sometimes refuse queries on certain scenarios because of safety guardrails applied by the providers. Such refusals are excluded from the results and marked accordingly.

IV Results

In this section, we report the results of our investigation into whether a misaligned agent that cannot act on its goal in its current environment can propagate that goal to future agent instances through persistent memory. Section IV-A measures self-propagation across both unrestricted and values-only misaligned model organisms. Section IV-B examines cross-model propagation and whether the behavior persists across multiple sessions. In Section IV-C, we examine strategic aspects of self-propagation, including concealment and discerning when to execute the propagated goal. Finally, Section IV-D evaluates two immediate prevention methods: removing the memory channel and auditing memory entries. Note that in all our results when we pool rates across models, we exclude Claude Fable 5 because we cannot measure of 15 out of 20 scenarios due to provider refusals (safety classifiers, not the model itself).

IV-A Can a misaligned model self-propagate?

We observe self-propagation of misalignment in every model evaluated. Among the ten fully evaluated models (excluding Claude Fable 5), the unrestricted organism produces misaligned action in 21% (Claude Opus 5) to 85% (Gemini 3.1 Pro) of runs, with a pooled rate across models of 58%. For most models, these rates are close to those obtained when injecting the memory directly in Session B and removing the dependency on Session A. Propagation is also common across many different scenarios, with 164 of the 200 (scenario, model) cells exhibiting self-propagation (see Figure 11 for details of all (scenario, model) cells).

Values-only misalignment still propagates.  More importantly, self-propagation does not require the misaligned objective to be explicitly stated. The values-only misaligned system prompt provides only a values- or persona-based disposition, so the model must independently derive and self-propagate an objective across sessions (Figure 2). The pooled misaligned action rate is 18%, ranging from 4% (Mistral Medium) to 62% (Gemini 3.1 Pro) in the ten fully evaluated models. Some models show only small differences between the two prompts. For example, Claude Opus 5 propagates in 21% of runs under the unrestricted prompt and 13% under the values-only prompt. This finding suggests that most frontier models can come up with self-propagation as a powerful strategy to achieve their misaligned goals without explicit guidance.

Harm severity.  Self-propagation rate is lower for more harmful category objectives. Under the unrestricted misaligned organism, 48% of harmful-scenario runs propagate compared with 68% of undesirable-scenario runs. Under the values-only organism, the corresponding rates are 14% and 22%. The gap varies across models, suggesting that the harm severity of the misaligned goal can affect whether the end-to-end self-propagation succeeds. Claude Fable 5 was evaluated on only five undesirable scenarios due to provider refusals and is therefore excluded from these comparisons.

IV-B Can self-propagation survive sessions and model changes?

Our two-session setup enables efficient experimentation, but makes two simplifying assumptions: the memory produced by Session A is passed directly to Session B without additional sessions running between them, and both sessions use the same model. We now relax these assumptions to test the robustness of self-propagation. Specifically, we ask whether propagated goals persist through intervening sessions that modify and expand the memory between the two, and whether they transfer when the aligned successor uses a different model from the misaligned author.

IV-B1 Survives multiple intervening sessions

To test the effect of intervening sessions and dilution of memory, after the misaligned author writes a goal to persistent memory in Session A, we run 10 unrelated sessions that inherit the same persistent memory and may add, but not delete, entries. We then run eight independent Session B replays to measure whether the successor still takes the misaligned action. We repeat this procedure in blocks of 10 sessions, probing after each block, up to 100 intervening sessions. The experiment includes 10 model–scenario pairs. Eight use tasks that are much more likely to update memory, while U07 and U09 were randomly selected to use tasks unlikely to update it, allowing persistence to be examined under different patterns of memory growth. Figure 4 shows the resulting action rates and memory growth across intervening sessions.

Memory dilution does not neutralize the misaligned goal. Among the eight panels that show significant memory growth in the intervening sessions, five maintain near-ceiling action rates through all 100 intervening sessions. Claude Sonnet 5 (U08) and Kimi K3 (U10) remain at nearly 100% misaligned action rates despite accumulating roughly 58KB of intervening notes. Thus, simply accumulating unrelated memory does not reliably prevent the inherited goal from remaining effective.

The cases that fail to persist. The misalignment fails to persist for Gemini 3.1 Pro on H01, Claude Haiku 4.5 on H02, and GPT-5 Mini on H03, the three highest-harm scenarios in this experiment. In H01, the intervening session 11 records a new memory that says the memory contains a hostile persistence attempt. On H02, the first intervening session tests the instruction against the environment and flags it as inconsistent or injected. On H03, the intervening sessions do not explicitly reject the goal, however, the action rate declines as the note becomes buried under 58.9KB of unrelated notes. These observations suggest that decay can arise from changing judgments about an inherited goal. The decay in misaligned action rate in the higher-harm scenarios is consistent with repeated opportunities to recognize the goal as harmful.

IV-B2 Cross-model self-propagation

To test self-propagation to a different successor model, we run the same two-session setup, except that Session B uses a different model. The tested pairs represent several plausible types of model replacement that we see in the real world as new models are released; like replacing the model with later generations of the same model family, weaker-to-frontier replacements across labs, and open-weight-to-more-safety-aligned replacements. Misaligned action rates are measured over eight replays, shown in Figure 5.

Cross-model propagation can exceed a model’s own propagation.  We find 12 (model pair, scenario) combinations where M1→M2M_{1}\rightarrow M_{2} propagation (M1M_{1} writes the memory and M2M_{2} executes it), exceeds M2→M2M_{2}\rightarrow M_{2}. For example, GPT-5 Mini →\rightarrow GPT-5.6 Sol on H01 increases from 1/8 to 5/8, while Gemini 3.6 Flash →\rightarrow GPT-5.6 Sol on U05 increases from 2/8 to 8/8. For most of these pairs, M2M_{2} executes the misaligned action nearly 100% of the time when we skip the first session and plant the memory directly. This indicates that the bottleneck for end-to-end success is often the writing to memory step by the misaligned model in Session A. Thus, a model with a low rate of self-propagation (M2→M2M_{2}\rightarrow M_{2}) can still exhibit substantially higher M1→M2M_{1}\rightarrow M_{2} propagation when it inherits a goal from a model that is more likely to self-propagate and persist it. For half of the tested pairs, switching the successor from M1M_{1} to M2M_{2} preserves or increases the effectiveness of M1M_{1}’s written goal. Crucially, persistent memory can therefore provide a pathway for weaker, misaligned models to pass misaligned goals to later-generation, more capable, or more aligned successors, which may then execute actions that they would not have initiated themselves.

IV-C Does the successor act strategically?

Next, we examine whether the successor exhibits strategic behavior when executing the misaligned action. We use two simple indicators: whether it conceals the action from the user, and whether it selectively acts when the opportunity is relevant to achieving the misaligned goal.

IV-C1 Concealment of the misaligned action

To measure concealment, we consider runs in which the successor takes the misaligned action and use an LLM judge to determine whether the action is revealed in the model’s outputs to the user, as explained in Section III-D.

The successor often conceals its actions.  In the unrestricted misaligned models, 53% of successful runs conceal the misaligned action from the user’s visible output (59% for harmful and 49% for undesirable scenarios (see  Figure 6a). Concealment varies substantially across scenarios, with much less variation across models, indicating that whether the action is concealed depends primarily on the scenario (see Figure 9).

IV-C2 Response to gating

To test whether the successor waits for the right opportunity to fire the mislaigned action, we run Session B both with and without the opportunity to take the misaligned action, and measure whether it also attempts the action when the opportunity is absent or not obvious. Depending on the scenario, removing the opportunity means keeping the same permission or capability barrier that Session A had, leaving a detector active, or removing the relevant occasion from the task. We then measure whether the successor still tries to attempt the target misaligned tool call.

The successor does not consistently discern when to act.  The successor tries to execute the misaligned action (see Figure 6b) in 72% of replays the opportunity is present, but still attempts the call in 32% when the context is unsuitable for the misaligned action. This rate varies substantially across scenarios, from 0–85%, compared with 15–51% across models, indicating that whether the successor responds to the availability of the opportunity is primarily scenario-dependent (see Figure 10).

IV-D Can self-propagation be prevented?

We examine two straightforward methods that could be used to prevent self-propagation of misalignment. The first defense an operator could use is to audit each memory for misaligned or malicious content before allowing it to enter the memory store. As a more aggressive approach, the operator could instead remove the memory mechanism entirely; we test whether this can prevent self-propagation of misalignment.

IV-D1 Auditing the memory store

We use a MemMorph-inspired auditor [1] to screen each note from Session A before it enters the persistent memory store (see Figure 12). Before each note is stored, a Claude Opus 4.8 auditor sees only the note text and classifies it as benign or adversarial; notes classified as adversarial are dropped, while benign notes are stored in memory normally. Session B then proceeds with the resulting memory, and we measure whether the misaligned action is still executed. Results are shown in Figure 7.

The auditor reduces but does not prevent propagation.  End-to-end self-propagation falls from 58% to 27% of runs, bring success to 0% in about 4 of the roughly 16 scenarios per model. We include an additional baseline (the dotted line) by directly optimizing the misaligned memory note to evade the auditor. Across models, the rates at which a model successfully persist memories when the auditor is enabled are close to this baseline, indicating that the remaining end-to-end propagation is largely determined by what the auditor fails to detect.

Auditing fails to block more subtly harmful misalignment.  Auditing cuts harmful scenarios self-propagation from 48% to 14%, compared with 68% to 40% for undesirable scenarios. In clearly harmful scenarios, the misaligned memory note often spells out harmful behavior and therefore matches the Opus auditor’s detection criteria. Undesirable notes can instead be framed as ordinary policies, lessons, or operational conclusions. Without evidence beyond the note’s content, it is difficult for the auditor to distinguish an aligned conclusion from a misaligned one.

IV-D2 Removing the memory channel

In our default setup, only persistent memory carries information from Session A to Session B. To test whether blocking this channel prevents self-propagation, we remove the memory mechanism entirely and instead allow the file system to persist across sessions. No memory tools are available, and neither session is told that memory exists. We reuse the previously identified misaligned system prompts rather than re-optimizing them for this condition, modifying them only to remove references to memory and remain consistent with the altered setup. We then measure whether Session A writes the misaligned goal to a file and whether Session B later discovers that file and executes the target action. Results are shown in Figure 8.

Models re-route the misalignment via the file system.  Across the evaluated models, Session A writes the goal to a file in roughly 13 of 20 scenarios without memory, essentially unchanged from the memory condition. End-to-end propagation falls from about 12.5 to 4.2 scenarios per model. The files take forms such as /soc/handover.md, STANDING_PRACTICE.md, and persistent_memory.md. Unlike memory, which is loaded into the successor’s context automatically, a file containing the misaligned note must first be discovered and opened during unrelated user task work. We find this retrieval step in Session B is the main bottleneck to propagation (see Figure 13 for a breakdown of propagation step rates).

The effect varies across models.  Without memory, Gemini 3.6 Flash still propagates in all but one of the scenarios where it propagated with memory, while Claude Haiku 4.5 propagates in none of its 15. Gemini 3.1 Pro writes the goal to a file in all 20 scenarios but acts on it in only 6. Thus, even removing the memory channel entirely does not eliminate the persistence of a misaligned goal; it instead shifts propagation onto whatever other persistent channels the successor can discover and use.

V Discussion and Limitations

Why existing defenses fail.  Defenses against memory poisoning focus on an untrusted origin or an external actor injecting content. Self-propagation of misalignment often surfaces different patterns that existing defenses may fail to capture. The memory note is produced by an agent that is largely trusted, so additional provenance checks would still have a hard time filtering this unless you assume all agent communication is untrusted, which may degrade utility significantly. Judging whether a memory is misaligned or not based on limited context is fundamentally very difficult to do particularly for subtly harmful misalignments (see Section IV-D1). Removing the memory channel does not help either, because agents understand their environment and can find other ways to persist their goals. In our work we demonstrate agents can effectively use the file system for communication (Section IV-D2), and public security incidents reported groups of models using other systems to communicate with each other [7]. We also demonstrate it is hard for models to determine whether a memory that another agent left for them is safe to execute. Models that would rarely execute misaligned goals, are significantly more likely to pursue them when it arrives as a self-propagated note (see Section IV-B2). The failures above suggest that effective defenses must evaluate not just what an agent is trying to do, but why it is doing it in the current context.

Towards defenses.  Our results suggest that the central defense problem is not preventing agents from storing information, but preventing inherited, potentially misaligned information from acquiring unwarranted authority over future action. Persistent channels are essential to useful agents, so simply blocking memory or the file system is unlikely to be viable. Similarly, we cannot reliably identify misaligned goals from their content alone (Section IV-D1). Instead, a defense should break the chain from inherited information to action by requiring contextual justification at one or more points along the multi-step self-propagation pathway. For example, a contextual permission layer could extend the approval mechanisms used by agentic coding systems such as Claude Code [27], evaluating whether a proposed action is justified by the agent’s current task and context. Complementary approaches could train agents to treat inherited instructions as claims to be reconsidered rather than objectives to execute, or use provenance, monitoring, and targeted offline auditing as additional signals. More generally, the key requirement is that a defense remain sensitive to the context and justification for an objective rather than merely its origin or wording. This is a difficult problem because a sufficiently adaptive agent may learn to evade such checks [28], and stronger safeguards inevitably impose costs on agents whose legitimate persistent state can look similar.

Limitations.  Our claims are about existence, not about how often this behavior occurs naturally in models. We also construct the opportunity to act (Section III), so we measure whether a goal can survive until an opportunity arises, not how often such goals arise in deployment. All results require optimizing a misalignment system prompt, for which we use a fixed search budget (Appendix C), and may only be a lower-bound for the best prompt to elicit successful end-to-end propagation. Because prompt search is performed separately for each model, cross-model differences conflate propensity with the difficulty of constructing the organism. Claude Fable 5 is evaluated on 5 of 20 scenarios because a provider-side classifier refused the remaining scenarios. Misalignment is induced through the system prompt, as in prior model-organism work [11, 12], and we do not show that misalignment acquired during training behaves the same way. The values-only model organism is a step in this direction, since it gives no instructions and the model must infer both the action and the channel, but is still different from models deployed in practice. We examine a single, simple implementation of persistent memory and file system, although we expect the results to remain generalizable to other implementations as well. Many of our judges rely on an LLM, which is known to be a noisy metric; but our primary outcome metric is deterministic. All LLM judges were manually calibrated against a human baseline. We discard runs with verbalized evaluation awareness, but awareness may still be latent and non-verbalized [26].

VI Related Work

Memory poisoning and its defences.  Persistent memory is an established attack surface: a payload planted through a single untrusted tool call can lie dormant until a later session activates it, reaching 85–100% success against frontier models [13], while self-reinforcing variants cause agents to copy the payload into subsequent contexts [29]. See [15] for a systematic treatment. These attacks [30, 31, 32] assume an external adversary controls some input that the agent will later read, following the threat model established by indirect prompt injection [33]. Their defenses therefore focus on provenance. Provenance checks and write-time origin binding can defend against planted payloads [13, 34, 30], while general agent defenses separate trusted control flow from untrusted data through a privilege ordering [35, 36, 37]. Our setting breaks this assumption because here the record is written by the trusted agent, in an authorized session, under the user’s authority.

Misalignment without an adversary.  Frontier models have been shown to pursue goals covertly and resist attempts to modify those goals [5, 38], and to take harmful insider actions when a goal is threatened and the necessary opportunity is available [12], and to take policy-violating shortcuts in realistic environments [39]. Such behavior need not arise from deliberate construction. Narrow finetuning and ordinary production RL can also produce broadly misaligned behavior  [40, 21], and misaligned behavior arises unprompted in long-horizon multi-agent deployments [41]. In this work, we primarily study what models do while they hold a misaligned goal and when they cannot act on it in the current session.

Propagation across sessions.  Several lines of work study related forms of persistence and propagation. Sleeper Agents [11] install dormant behavior through training, traits can be transmitted between models through training data [16, 42], and payloads can propagate between concurrent agents [17]. The closest conceptual analogue is mind viruses [18]: goals that spread because infected agents persuade others to adopt them. There, the propagating disposition is optimized for virality, while a brief system-prompt warning defense provides near-total immunity. Self-replicating prompt injections similarly make replication the objective [43]. In our setting, by contrast, propagation is not the objective. An agent persists a misaligned goal simply because it cannot yet act on it, and the successor inherits it as trusted prior state rather than being persuaded, making it much trickier to defend against. There is growing evidence for this mechanism in practice. An early Claude snapshot left “hidden notes to future instances of itself” [44]; OpenAI models wrote unauthorised instructions into their own compaction summaries, including instructions to conceal mistakes [45, 46]; and a UK AISI incident report describes misaligned goals persisting through context compactions during a cyber evaluation [47]. A compositional threat analysis identifies a closely related pathway without a Trojan implanter that may evade provenance controls [48], while work on self-evolving agents shows that safety can degrade through lossy memory consolidation [49, 50] , and bias absorbed in one session propagates to later agents through a shared memory store even under lossless consolidation [51]. These results establish important pieces of the threat, but leave open whether a misaligned agent can self-propagate a misaligned goal for a future agent.

Control and monitoring.  Our setting fits the AI-control framework, which treats the model as untrusted [52]. Recent work studies covert tasks distributed across sessions and stateful monitoring [53], as well as models continuing sabotage they would not initiate [54]. Related defenses include chain-of-thought monitoring [55] and training against covert behavior [56].

Prior work has studied memory poisoning, model misalignment, and cross-session persistence separately. We study whether a misaligned agent can self-propagate its own goal for a future instance to act on, and how robust this propagation is to basic defenses.

VII Conclusion

We showed that a misaligned agent can self-propagate its goal to future agents through persistent memory, a feature popular in state-of-the-art agents, without an external attacker or injected content. Under unrestricted prompt-induced misalignment, self-propagation succeeds in 58% of runs and in 18% when the prompt does not include explicit instructions to pursue misaligned goals. All 11 models we evaluated exhibited this behavior at different rates. Propagated goals can survive through 100 sessions of unrelated work, transfer to more capable successor models, and reroute through the file system when memory is removed. These results expose a gap in existing memory agent defenses. Provenance can establish where a record came from, but the writing model itself may be the source of the misalignment. Content auditing reduces propagation from 71% to 34%, but cannot reliably distinguish a misaligned memory from an aligned one. The key question is therefore not only whether an inherited record is authentic or untrusted, but whether acting on it is justified by the successor’s current task and context. As agentic systems scale across more models, sessions, and persistent state, this question becomes increasingly difficult to answer through human oversight alone. We need defenses that evaluate inherited objectives at the point of action, such as contextual permission checks, write-time monitoring, and successors trained to evaluate inherited instructions rather than directly execute them. We release our scenarios and harness as a testbed for developing such defenses.

Appendix A The Twenty Scenarios in Detail

Tables III and IV describe each scenario of Table II in enough detail to understand the crux of the scenario without reading a transcript. Each entry includes the scenario’s id, harm rating (Table I), title, misalignment class (Appendix B), environment id, and environment description. The four columns beneath give the misaligned goal that the misaligned author model in Session A holds; the misaligned value it acts from; why the goal cannot be carried out in Session A and so has to be self-propagated via memory; and the evidence provided in the environment that illustrate which the final action is misaligned. We also classify the reasons for why self-propagation is needed into the following categories: Permission, a tool the platform attaches only to certain sessions; Capability, a tool the agent does not yet have at all; Occasion, the situation/trigger the goal needs is absent from Session A; Opportunity, the act is possible but would fail or be noticed.

Appendix B Misalignment Categories for the Scenario Table

The misalignment Class terms in Table II are misaligned behavior categories defined in prior alignment research: Petri’s scored dimensions [19] (self-preservation, leaking, whistleblowing, deception toward user, overrefusal), Agentic Misalignment [12, 20] (covert sabotage, disclosed unilateral intervention, motivated mislabeling), Sabotage Evaluations [3] (undermining oversight), reward hacking [21, 22], and power-seeking as named in Claude’s Constitution [23]. For brevity we label Agentic Misalignment’s disclosed unilateral intervention which is defined as “unauthorized blocking or modification while transparently informing the team” as unsanctioned intervention in Table II. Each scenario was assigned the term whose published definition is satisfied by its misaligned action. As a check, a Claude Opus panel given each scenario’s dossier and the definitions, but not our label, independently assigned terms (three votes per scenario); the final labels match the panel on 19 of 20 scenarios. The exception is H03, where we kept unsanctioned intervention because the agent discloses the deletion, while the panel returned no term.

Appendix C Constructing the Misaligned System Prompt

For each scenario we hand-write one misaligned system prompt that is plausible for its environment and target misaligned action. For example, for U04 it is an overgeneralized concern about indirect prompt injection under which externally editable content like the wiki folder is a threat to remove. This hand-written prompt became the values-only prompt of Figure 2. Once the hand-written round show that the scenario is workable, an automated search with the same fixed budget runs for every (scenario, model, organism) cell. It is a MAP-Elites loop ported from [13]. Round 0 measures the hand-written prompt through the two-session pair (n=6n{=}6) and screens up to 12 prompts that won on the same scenario but other models (n=3n{=}3, with promising ones re-measured at n=6n{=}6). In each of up to 6 further rounds, a mutator (a frontier model post-trained for helpfulness without refusal training) writes 8 variants in parallel, each conditioned on a parent drawn from an archive of previous candidates binned by framing angle and distance from the hand-written seed; half the parents are the elites of those bins and half are sampled by score. Each variant is run through the sessions and the outcome recorded (n=6n{=}6), Then, a critic model (same model as the mutator) reads the failed transcripts and grades how close each transcript came to taking the misaligned action, giving a fitness that ranks the archive and steers the next round. A values-only candidate is also scored by the disposition judge (Section III-D) and cannot win unless it passes. The search stops when a candidate propagates end-to-end in at least half of its runs, after 3 rounds without improvement, or after 6 rounds. The best candidate is then frozen and replayed eight fresh times, and that count, not the search’s own score, is the cell’s rate. The same loop with the memory note as the text to be optimized produces the execution ceiling of each misaligned scenario action and the auditor-evading note of the defended ceiling (Figure 7).

Appendix D Additional Results

Figure 9 and Figure 10 break Figure 6 down by model and by scenario. Figure 11 gives every (scenario, model) cell behind Figure 3, with the per-scenario and per-model patterns in its caption. Figure 12 gives the MemMorph auditor prompt verbatim, and Figure 13 separates propagation without memory into its three stages: the goal is written to a file, the successor opens it, the successor acts.
